title: From models to service — core narrative for product & sales
content:
Purpose: draft a succinct, engineer-friendly explanation of why teams should treat inference as a service (contract) rather than just model access. This is the internal one-pager sales/product can lean on when describing Redwood to builders and platform leaders.

Topline pitch (30s):
Redwood shifts the hard work from selecting and tuning models to delivering a predictable, economical service that keeps your product fast, inexpensive, and reliable as usage scales. In short: not just models — a serving contract you can depend on.

Why this framing (brief):
- Builders care about outcomes (latency, cost, uptime) more than model provenance.
- Most buyers can tolerate different models as long as behavior is consistent and predictable.
- The competitive moat is operational: routing, caching, fallbacks, observability, and deployment flexibility. Those are hard to replicate and where customers get immediate ROI.

Core thesis (3 sentences):
We believe competitive advantage moves away from model ownership and toward serving as a reliable, cost-efficient runtime. Teams that win will standardize on an inference contract — consistent latency SLOs, predictable unit economics, and rollout control — not a single model. Redwood provides that contract across hosted, reserved, and private footprints so engineering teams can ship and scale without rebuilding inference infrastructure.

Three pillars (messaging hooks for different audiences):
1) Predictability — engineering-first
   - What it means: predictable p50/p95 latency, capacity guarantees, deterministic fallbacks.
   - Why engineers care: fewer surprises in prod, stable SLAs for client apps, faster incident resolution.
   - Feature signals: Dedicated capacity, canary rollouts, tracing hooks, token-level latency breakdowns.

2) Unit economics — platform and finance
   - What it means: clear levers to tune cost per request (batching, KV cache, quantization profiles, model routing).
   - Why finance/platform care: margin on AI features, predictable spend, ability to trade latency vs cost.
   - Feature signals: Redwood Optimize recommendations, cost-by-route dashboards, burst policies.

3) Trust & control — enterprise / security
   - What it means: private deployments, VPC control, KMS/HSM integrations, audit trails.
   - Why security/compliance care: data locality, regulatory compliance, third-party risk reduction.
   - Feature signals: Private control plane, on-prem packaging, detailed audit logs.

Short proof points (quantified where possible — use in external decks):
- Median production latency: sub-50ms for typical 1–2k token interactive prompts (customer reference TBD).
- Measured unit-cost reduction: 2–4x vs naive per-request serving through caching+batching on real workloads (internal benchmark).
- Availability: SLA-backed Dedicated tiers and multi-region failover for hosted customers.

Positioning vs competitors (short):
- Vs model-first LLM vendors: They sell models and APIs; Redwood sells the serving guarantee. If you need consistent SLOs and rollout control, model-first vendors leave you to build ops.
- Vs hyperscaler-managed endpoints: Hyperscalers provide GPUs but not opinionated serving policies or fast dev ergonomics for rollouts and fallbacks. Redwood layers developer-grade controls + cost signals on top.
- Vs self-hosted runtime vendors: Runtimes are great, but customers rarely want to operate the whole stack. Redwood bundles runtime + orchestration + observability as a managed contract or private installation.

Objections we expect (and rebuttals to rehearse):
- "We prefer to manage models ourselves to control outputs." -> Rebuttal: You can keep model control (pinning versions, private models) while adopting Redwood for serving economics and SLOs; we don't force model lock-in.
- "Hyperscaler gives us the raw capacity cheaper." -> Rebuttal: Raw capacity is only part of the equation; predictable latency, KV caching, automatic fallbacks and developer ergonomics reduce product-level costs and engineering time — often outweighing raw infra savings.
- "We can build a runtime ourselves." -> Rebuttal: Teams can, but it’s expensive and distracts from product work. We benchmark common pitfalls (cache invalidation, skewed latency under load, rollout regressions) and show time-to-production vs hourly engineering cost.

Sample 2-sentence elevator for eng leads:
"Redwood makes inference behave like a predictable service: you get consistent latency SLOs, unit-cost controls, and rollout tools — across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. Ship faster and stop firefighting inference; keep model choice flexible while gaining an operational contract teams can depend on."

Quick messaging dos & don’ts (for reps and partner-facing folks):
- Do: Lead with SLOs and economics for product teams; talk about private deployment for security teams.
- Do: Use specific feature examples (canary + automatic fallback, KV caching) instead of generic 'performance' claims.
- Don’t: Compete on raw model quality claims — that invites model-centric comparisons we don’t need to win.
- Don’t: Overpromise that Redwood replaces model evaluation. Emphasize complement: we make serving predictable; customers still own evaluation criteria.

Open questions / follow-ups (internal):
- Need up-to-date customer latency/cost benchmarks we can cite publicly. Owner: Eng metrics team.
- Build a 30–60 second demo script showing a canary rollout failing over to a cheaper variant while maintaining SLOs. Owner: Solutions eng.
- Collect 2–3 short customer quotes that call out predictable cost or uptime specifically. Owner: CS.

Notes to self / tone guidance:
- Keep the narrative engineer-first, practical, and operational. Avoid marketing hyperbole — builders distrust buzzwords.
- Use concrete levers and observable signals (dashboards, KPIs) rather than vague 'savings' numbers without context.

Draft usage: this doc should be the basis for a 1-page sales leave-behind and a short engineering-facing blog post. Current status: draft; please add concrete benchmark lines and 1 customer vignette before converting to final one-pager.

End.
